paragraphs.heading: The mathematics of straight things
paragraphs.text: Linear algebra is the branch of mathematics about linear equations, about linear maps, and about how both are represented with vector spaces and matrices. It sits at the center of almost every area of mathematics. Modern geometry uses it even to define lines, planes and rotations.

paragraphs.heading: Why scientists need it
paragraphs.text: Most sciences and branches of engineering use linear algebra, since many physical phenomena are naturally modeled by linear structures; it is useful across computing too. Even for nonlinear systems it helps: near a point, a curved shape can be modeled by a line given by its derivative, and that line can be studied with linear algebra.

paragraphs.heading: Vectors and scalars
paragraphs.text: The central object is a vector space: a set V together with a field F of numbers, often the real or complex numbers. Members of V are called vectors and members of F are called scalars. It comes with two operations: adding two vectors v and w to get v + w, and multiplying a vector v by a scalar a to get av. Vectors can be many things, such as tuples, sequences, functions, polynomials or matrices, and linear algebra studies what all of them have in common.

paragraphs.heading: Maps between spaces
paragraphs.text: A linear map that pairs every vector of one space with exactly one vector of another is called an isomorphism. Two spaces linked this way are essentially the same, since no vector space property can tell them apart. A key question is whether a given map is an isomorphism; if not, one looks for its range and its kernel, the set of vectors it sends to zero.

paragraphs.heading: From counting rods to Cramer
paragraphs.text: The method now called Gaussian elimination, done with counting rods, appears in the ancient Chinese text The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art. In Europe, René Descartes brought coordinates into geometry in 1637, so lines and planes became linear equations and finding where they cross meant solving a system. Leibniz first used determinants for this in 1693, and in 1750 Gabriel Cramer used them to write explicit solutions, now called Cramer's rule.

paragraphs.heading: Matrices get a name
paragraphs.text: In 1848 James Joseph Sylvester coined the term matrix, Latin for womb. In 1856 Arthur Cayley introduced matrix multiplication and the inverse matrix, and he wrote a whole matrix as a single letter, treating it as one object. Peano gave the first modern, precise definition of a vector space in 1888.

paragraphs.heading: The modern form
paragraphs.text: Linear algebra took its modern shape in the first half of the twentieth century, as older ideas were generalized into abstract algebra. Computers then drove research into fast algorithms for Gaussian elimination and matrix decompositions, making the subject essential for modeling and simulation. Until the 19th century it was taught through equations and matrices; today the vector space approach is usually preferred, as more general and conceptually simpler, though more abstract.
